title: Flexible Spending Account (FSA): The Ultimate Guide
summary: Learn how a flexible spending account (FSA) works, how much you can save on taxes, what expenses qualify, and how to avoid losing unused FSA funds.
body_markdown:
A flexible spending account lets you set aside pre-tax money from your paycheck to pay for medical expenses and dependent care expenses you already expect to incur. If your employer offers one, it is one of the fastest ways to lower your tax bill without changing how you spend on health care.


## What Is a Flexible Spending Account (FSA)?


A flexible spending account FSA is an employer-sponsored, tax-advantaged financial account that lets employees contribute pre-tax dollars toward eligible healthcare and dependent care costs. Because FSA contributions are deducted from your paycheck before federal income, Social Security, and Medicare taxes are calculated, employees can save on taxes immediately. The result is lower taxable income and higher take-home pay on every pay period.


FSAs are governed by[Section 125 of the Internal Revenue Code](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15b) , which means only employers can offer them as part of a cafeteria benefits plan. About 47% of private-industry workers currently have access to a healthcare FSA, according to the[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/ebs/factsheets/flexible-benefits-in-the-workplace.htm) . If you leave your job, FSA funds typically stay with your employer unless you qualify for COBRA continuation.


There are two primary types. Healthcare FSAs cover out-of-pocket medical, dental, and vision expenses. Dependent care FSAs cover childcare costs and certain adult day care so household members can work. Most plans follow a "use-it-or-lose-it" rule: unused FSA funds at the end of the plan year (plus any grace period) are forfeited, though some employers allow a small carryover into the next year. Flex helps people actually spend these dollars by making it easy to[shop FSA-eligible products and pay directly with an FSA card](https://www.withflex.com/) .


Key features at a glance:


- An FSA can cover a wide range of out-of-pocket health care costs, from copays to prescriptions to contact lenses
- Contributions are pre-tax, reducing your earnings subject to federal income, FICA taxes, and often state taxes
- Annual contribution limits for FSAs are set by the IRS and adjusted periodically
- Employer plans determine specifics like eligible expenses, administrative rules, and whether a carryover or grace period applies
- FSAs operate only through employer-sponsored Section 125 cafeteria plans


## Tax Savings and How FSAs Work in Practice


The core benefit of a flexible spending account is tax savings for both the employee and employer. FSA contributions reduce taxable income before taxes are deducted, which means every dollar you contribute bypasses federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare taxes. Employers also avoid their matching portion of payroll taxes (about 7.65% of the contributed amount), which offsets the cost of administering the plan.


Here is how the mechanics and savings break down:


- During open enrollment, you elect an annual contribution. That amount is divided evenly across pay periods and deducted from pre-tax money each paycheck. For Healthcare FSAs, you get access to the full elected amount on day one of the plan year, even though deductions happen over time.
- A 2026 example: an employee earning $60,000 who contributes $3,000 to a Healthcare FSA reduces taxable wages to $57,000. At a combined tax rate of roughly 25%, that yields about $750 in tax savings. Employees in the 22% tax bracket save about $440 on $2,000 in contributions.
- An employee contributing $5,000 to a Dependent Care FSA saves $1,500 in taxes at a 30% combined rate. Dependent care FSAs can cover up to $5,000 annually for childcare, with a lower limit for married filing separately.
- Employees save on federal income taxes with FSA contributions, and those same pre-tax contributions also reduce Social Security and Medicare taxes owed.
- FSA contributions reduce taxable income, increasing take-home pay without requiring a raise or a change in spending habits.
- Compare at a glance: using pre-tax dollars through a flexible spending account for eligible health and care expenses can feel like paying 20-30% less, because those funds bypass income and payroll taxes entirely.


## Types of Flexible Spending Accounts and Eligible Expenses


Healthcare FSAs and dependent care FSAs each have their own rules, contribution limits, and lists of eligible expenses. Understanding the difference prevents claim denials and wasted funds.


- Healthcare FSAs reimburse out-of-pocket medical expenses for the employee, spouse, and tax dependents. Healthcare FSAs cover copayments and prescription medications, along with deductibles, coinsurance, and many over-the-counter products (which the IRS confirmed as eligible under Code section 213(d)).
- Eligible medical expenses include vision care and dental procedures: eye exams, prescription glasses and sunglasses, contact lenses, hearing aids, dental cleanings, fillings, orthodontia, and diagnostic tests. Physical therapy, mental health counseling, and prescriptions also qualify. See Flex's[complete list of 220+ FSA eligible items](https://www.withflex.com/blog/fsa-eligible-items-list) for a full breakdown.
- Many everyday wellness products are FSA-eligible when used for a diagnosed medical condition. Flex's marketplace[curates HSA/FSA-eligible products like fitness and recovery tools, sleep products, skincare for specific conditions, women's health devices, and vision expenses products that qualify](https://www.withflex.com/category/all) .
- Dependent Care FSAs reimburse qualified dependent care expenses that enable household members to work, look for work, or attend school full time. Dependent care FSAs cover childcare costs for children under 13, before- and after-school programs, eligible day camps, nursery school, and certain adult day care for disabled dependents who live with you.
- Employees can contribute up to $5,000 annually for dependent care ($2,500 if married filing separately). Parents who rely on daycare or after-school care can offset a meaningful portion of those childcare costs with pre-tax contributions.
- Ineligible expenses: FSA funds cannot reimburse health insurance premiums or cosmetic procedures. Overnight camps, tutoring, and care provided by a spouse or a child under age 19 are also excluded.


## Rules, Deadlines, and Common Flexible Spending Pitfalls


FSAs are a powerful tool, but they are rule-bound. In 2023, about half of FSA holders forfeited unused funds, with the average forfeiture running around $436 per account. Missteps in planning or timing cause most of these losses.


- Contribution limits: The IRS sets annual limits. For 2026, the Healthcare FSA maximum is $3,400 per employee. Dependent care FSAs allow up to $5,000 per household ($2,500 married filing separately). Employers can set lower caps but cannot exceed IRS regulations.
- Use-it-or-lose-it: Unused FSA funds may be forfeited under use-it-or-lose-it rules. Some employers offer a carryover of up to $660 into the next year, while others provide a[grace period of up to 2.5 months](https://www.withflex.com/blog/use-or-lose-fsa-expire) after the plan year ends. Plans cannot offer both for the same plan year.
- Enrollment timing: Open enrollment periods typically occur before the plan year begins, often in the fall for a January 1 start. You generally cannot change your FSA contribution mid-year unless a qualifying life event occurs, such as marriage, divorce, or the birth or adoption of a child.
- Common mistakes: overestimating predictable medical or dependent care expenses; confusing Healthcare FSAs with dependent care FSAs and submitting claims to the wrong account; spending funds on ineligible items; missing the plan's run-out deadline for submitting claims—issues that often show up in[customer support FAQs about HSA/FSA payments and reimbursements](https://docs.withflex.com/merchant-success/support/customer-support) .
- Documentation of eligible expenses may be required for[FSA reimbursement and how it works](https://www.withflex.com/blog/hsa-fsa-reimbursement-how-to) . Keep receipts, explanations of benefits, and provider statements. FSA debit card transactions often require follow-up proof; plans can suspend card access until documentation is submitted. Employees must submit claims within specific deadlines to avoid forfeiture.
- HSAs and FSAs have different rules regarding portability and contribution limits. A general Healthcare FSA disqualifies you from contributing to a health savings account unless your employer offers a limited purpose FSA covering only dental and vision. Always verify your plan's terms, especially if you want to use[HSA/FSA reimbursement for services like gyms, studios, and spas](https://www.withflex.com/business/product/reimbursement) .


## How to Use an FSA Strategically (and How Flex Helps You Spend Smarter)


Flexible spending works best when you treat it as a budgeting exercise, not a guess. Here is how to estimate, track, and spend FSA funds with precision.


- Estimate contributions by reviewing last year's healthcare and dependent care receipts. Factor in known upcoming changes: new prescriptions, planned surgeries, braces, or a child entering daycare. Choose a conservative number that captures recurring costs without overcommitting to the account.
- Track balances monthly through your employer's benefits portal. Set calendar reminders 90 days, 60 days, and 30 days before the plan year or grace period ends so you have time to spend remaining funds.
- Plan last-quarter purchases around[FSA-eligible health and wellness products](https://www.withflex.com/blog/how-to-use-fsa-funds-before-end-of-year) : extra contact lenses, prescription sunglasses, approved skincare for diagnosed conditions, sleep devices, over-the-counter medicines, and fitness recovery tools. These are expenses most people will incur anyway.

Eligibility is verified at checkout, reducing claim rejections.

- Coordinate your FSA with other benefits where allowed. If your employer offers a[health savings account](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) alongside an FSA, verify compatibility; a limited purpose FSA (dental and vision only) preserves HSA eligibility.
